title: Probability
cover_sub: Every outcome, every branch. Secure single events and expected results, extend to tree diagrams, then master without-replacement problems and algebra.

levels_long.s: Single events, missing probabilities, relative frequency, listing outcomes.
levels_long.e: Tree diagrams with replacement, combined events, counting, and tampered evidence.
levels_long.m: Without replacement, 'at least one', conditional probability and algebra.

briefing: Probabilities add up to 1. P(not A) = 1 − P(A). For independent events, multiply: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). For outcomes that can't happen together, add: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).
On a tree diagram, multiply along the branches and add between the routes you want. Without replacement, the second set of branches changes: one fewer item, and one fewer of the colour you took.
method: Write the probabilities on every branch. Each set of branches adds up to 1.
Multiply along each route you want.
For 'at least one', it's usually quicker to do 1 − P(none).

example.question: A bag has 3 red and 5 blue counters. Two are taken without replacement. Find the probability that both are red.
steps: First counter: P(red) = 38.
Without replacement there are now 2 red out of 7: P(red) = 27.
Multiply along the branch: 38 × 27 = 656.
Simplify: 328. Check: it's smaller than 38 × 38, as it should be ✓

s.blurb: The method, step by step. Show every line.

text: A bag has 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green counters. One is taken at random. Find P(blue).
Using the same bag, find P(red or green).
A spinner lands on A, B, C or D with probabilities 0.2, 0.35, x and 0.15. Find x.
A dice is thrown 200 times and lands on six 48 times. Estimate how many sixes there would be in 500 throws.
Two fair coins are flipped. List all the possible outcomes, and find P(two heads).
questions.answer: HH, HT, TH, TT; P(two heads) = 1/4
questions.tip: HT and TH are different outcomes. Missing one is the most common slip.

text: A bag has n sweets, 6 of them orange. Two are taken without replacement. P(both orange) = 1/3.
Show that n² − n − 90 = 0, and find n.
60% of a class study French. Of these, 30% also study Spanish. Of the others, 50% study Spanish. A student who studies Spanish is chosen at random. Find the probability they also study French.

closed_points: Use the fact that probabilities add up to 1.
Estimate with relative frequency and expected outcomes.
Draw and use tree diagrams: multiply along, add between.
Handle without-replacement problems by changing the second branches.
Use 1 − P(none), conditional probability and algebra.
